Project case study

Analytics Agent

A natural-language data analysis platform. Users upload a dataset and enter a prompt. An LLM interprets the request and elaborates a plan that maps to a list of available deterministic operations (tools). Then, the user has the opportunity to approve or cancel a plan. If they approve, the operations are performed on the data and an LLM interprets them and produces an overview of the most important points. Excel and PDF export are also available and automated, as well as other unique features such as chat and project roles, comments, multi-user chats and chat branching.

Architecture

The Tool interface — the contract the system runs on

backend/tools/tool.py · tool_registry.py

This is the contract that the system runs on. There is an abstract Tool interface that determines the tools' structure and that the tool registry is composed of. Each tool self-describes for the LLM planner (spec_for_llm), executes reproducibly (run), optionally reshapes data for the next plan step (transform), and renders itself into a report (to_export). New tools slot into the registry with zero changes to the agent or execution layers. Personally implemented the summary, correlation, and group-comparison tools on this interface.

# tool.py
class Tool(ABC):

    # 1. Self-description: every tool declares what it does and what its arguments represent
    @classmethod @abstractmethod
    def description(cls) -> str: ...
    @classmethod @abstractmethod
    def args(cls) -> list[tuple[str, str]]: ...

    #    spec_for_llm renders that into the prompt block the planner reads —
    #    the registry concatenates one per tool, so adding a tool  adding
    #    it to the planner's vocabulary
    @classmethod
    def spec_for_llm(cls) -> str:
        return name + description() + args()

    # 2. Deterministic execution: the LLM never touches the numbers
    @abstractmethod
    def run(self, data: Dataset, args: dict) -> dict: ...

    # 3. Composition: transform tools hand a reshaped dataset forward,
    #    so "filter to Software, then rank" ranks only the filtered rows
    def transform(self, data: Dataset, args: dict) -> Dataset | None:
        return None

    # 4. Reporting: every tool knows how to render itself into a Sheet 
      (a representation object later transformed into Excel/PDF)
    @classmethod
    def to_export(cls, result: dict, data: Dataset) -> Sheet: ...
View the registry's self-description — what the LLM planner actually sees (8 tools) 
■ Summary
  Return metadata summary of the dataset. Use no args to summarise all columns. Only specify `columns` if the user asks about specific columns.
    · columns: Optional list of column names to summarise. Omit to summarise all columns.

■ GroupComparison
  Aggregate a numeric metric across groups defined by a categorical column. Use when the user asks how a metric varies by category, which group has the highest or lowest value, or wants to rank or compare segments (e.g. by industry, tier, region, or banker). Always extract both a group_column and a metric_column from the user prompt. Default to 'mean' unless the user specifies otherwise or 'count' is more appropriate (e.g. 'how many deals per sector'). Pair with anova_test if the user also wants to know whether group differences are statistically significant.
    · group_column: Required. Categorical, binary, or discrete column whose unique values define the groups.
    · metric_column: Required. Numeric (continuous or discrete) column to aggregate within each group.
    · aggregation: Aggregation function to apply: 'mean', 'median', 'sum', or 'count'. Defaults to 'mean'.

■ CorrelationAnalysis
  Compute pairwise Pearson correlations between numeric columns. Use this tool when the user asks which columns are correlated, whether two variables are related, or wants to identify redundant features or multicollinearity before modelling. Do NOT use for categorical relationships — use chi_square_test instead. Only specify 'columns' if the user names specific columns; otherwise omit it and all numeric columns will be used. Raise threshold toward 0.7-0.9 for strong-only results; lower it toward 0.3 to surface weaker signals.
    · columns: Optional list of numeric column names to include. Omit to use all continuous and discrete columns in the dataset.
    · threshold: Minimum absolute correlation value (0-1) for a pair to appear in results. Defaults to 0.5. Lower to see weaker relationships; raise to focus on strong ones.

■ Filter
  Subset the dataset to the rows matching one or more conditions. Use when the user asks about a specific segment or slice of the data, or wants to narrow it down (e.g. 'companies in the Software sector', 'deals over $100M', 'rows since 2023'). Reports how many rows match, what fraction of the dataset that is, and returns a sample of the matching rows. Multiple conditions are combined with AND — every condition must hold. Do NOT use this to aggregate or rank; use GroupComparison for per-group metrics.
    · filters: Required. A list of condition objects, each {"column": <name>, "operator": <op>, "value": <value>}. Operators: '==', '!=' (any column); '>', '>=', '<', '<=' (numeric or datetime columns); 'in', 'not_in' (value must be a list); 'contains' (case-insensitive text substring match). All conditions are combined with AND.
    · limit: Optional. Maximum number of matching rows to return in the sample. Defaults to 20. The full match count is always reported regardless of this limit.

■ TrendAnalysis
  Aggregate a numeric metric over a date column into time buckets to show a trend. Use when the user asks how something changes over time, or wants a monthly/quarterly/yearly breakdown (e.g. 'revenue over time', 'deals per quarter', 'yearly average valuation'). Requires a datetime column; the metric column is required unless the aggregation is 'count' (which just counts rows per period). Reports one value per period in chronological order, plus a first-to-last trend summary. Use GroupComparison instead when comparing across categories rather than over time.
    · date_column: Required. A datetime column whose values are bucketed into periods.
    · metric_column: Numeric column to aggregate within each period. Required unless aggregation is 'count'.
    · period: Bucket size: 'D' (day), 'W' (week), 'M' (month), 'Q' (quarter), or 'Y' (year). Defaults to 'M'.
    · aggregation: How to combine values in each period: 'sum', 'mean', 'median', or 'count'. Defaults to 'sum'.

■ Ranking
  Sort the rows by a numeric or datetime column, optionally keeping only the top or bottom N. Use when the user wants the top or bottom N items, a ranking, the largest/smallest/most-recent/oldest records (e.g. 'top 10 clients by revenue', '5 largest deals'), OR simply the data sorted by a column with no cut-off (e.g. 'sort by revenue', 'order deals oldest first') — omit N for a full sort that keeps every row. Use GroupComparison instead when the user wants a per-category aggregate rather than specific rows.
    · column: Required. The numeric or datetime column to rank by.
    · n: Optional. How many rows to return. Omit to return ALL rows in sorted order (a full sort).
    · order: 'top' for the highest values (or most recent dates), 'bottom' for the lowest (or oldest). Defaults to 'top'.

■ SegmentComparison
  Compare ONE group's value of a numeric metric against the average of all OTHER groups combined. Use to quantify how far a single segment stands apart from the rest — e.g. 'how does Software's average revenue compare to every other sector combined?'. Ideal as a FOLLOW-UP once another analysis has surfaced a dominant or outlying group worth isolating. Requires a group_column, the specific group_value to isolate, and a numeric metric_column. Defaults to 'mean' unless another aggregation is specified.
    · group_column: Required. Categorical, binary, or discrete column whose values define the groups.
    · group_value: Required. The value in group_column to isolate as the segment; it is compared against all other values combined.
    · metric_column: Required. Numeric (continuous or discrete) column to aggregate for the segment and for the rest.
    · aggregation: Aggregation to apply: 'mean', 'median', 'sum', or 'count'. Defaults to 'mean'.

■ OutlierDetection
  Find rows whose value on a numeric column is a statistical outlier — far from the column's mean, measured in standard deviations (z-score). Use to surface unusual records that stand out from the norm (e.g. 'which companies have unusually high revenue?'). Because the outliers are not known until computed, this is a natural first step whose results can motivate a follow-up. Requires a numeric column; 'threshold' is the minimum absolute z-score to flag (default 2.0).
    · column: Required. Numeric (continuous or discrete) column to scan for outliers.
    · threshold: Minimum absolute z-score (standard deviations from the mean) to flag a row as an outlier. Defaults to 2.0.
    · label_column: Optional. Column used to identify each outlier row (e.g. a name or id). Defaults to the first column.
Data engineering

Data ingestion & parsing

backend/ingestion/ — dataset.py, parsers/, sourcers/

Ingestion layer: a Dataset object is extracted from the Excel upload using Panda's dataframes. This object then represents the parsed data the whole pipeline operates on. The architecture is built modularly such that there is availability to parse from different source sites (local file, Databricks, etc.) and from different source formats (Excel, PDF, etc), and these arrays of sites and inputs can be easily extended.

Below: the profile a Dataset computes on construction, produced by running the real pipeline (LocalSourcer → ExcelParser → Dataset) on a fictional Pitchbook-style file.

Reporting

Excel report generation

backend/export/ — sheet.py, exporter.py, excel_exporter.py

Every tool's structured result is rendered into a shared Sheet abstraction, which an exporter turns into a polished, consistently formatted .xlsx workbook under a strict style system, so every generated report looks identical regardless of the analysis that produced it.

Platform

State, persistence & the collaboration model

backend/data/ · backend/features/auth.py · branching.py · the State & Persistence Contract

Delta table clients over an SQL warehouse, Unity Catalog Volumes for files, schema checks, and a repository layer that keeps the FastAPI service fully stateless between requests. On top of it I designed the permission model and built key collaboration features:

  • Independent project-level and chat-level role systems (viewer / commentor / writer / manager / owner).
  • Storage-layer invariants — e.g. a CHECK constraint enforcing a chat is personal or project-published, never both
  • Dataset transformation lineage: every agent run appends the tools it applied, making analyses traceable end to end
  • Auth: header-based identity behind the Databricks Apps reverse proxy, with a deliberate no-fallback design — a missing header fails loudly with a 401 rather than silently attributing one user's data to a placeholder identity
  • Branching: copy-based chat branches that carry the parent's full history and record the branch point
Project roles — access to the feed
ViewerSees published chats and files; can start their own private chats in that context.
EditorEverything a viewer can do, plus publishing chats and files to the feed.
ManagerAdds and removes members — independent of viewer and editor access.
OwnerThe creator. Cannot be removed or demoted by any manager — only the owner can transfer ownership.
Chat roles — access to one conversation
ViewerReads the conversation and its results; can branch their own copy.
CommentorEverything a viewer can do, plus comments on any message.
WriterCo-author: adds questions and turns. Does not imply any management rights.
ManagerManages access to this chat. Granted per chat — never inherited from the project.
OwnerThe creator. Cannot be removed or demoted by any manager — only the owner can transfer ownership.
Product design

Interface concepts I designed

The frontend was implemented by my teammate; several of its defining product concepts were mine. These turned a single-player analytics chat into a shared analytical workspace:

Multi-user chats

Multiple writers co-authoring one analysis chat, with live presence — analysis as a shared workspace rather than a private conversation.

Publish to project feed

Private chats can be published to a project's shared feed, with publishing rights governed by project roles — how finished analyses reach the team.

Branch divider

A branched chat marks the boundary between copied history and its own new turns — answering "why does this chat have history I didn't write?" exactly where the question arises.

Margin comments (co-designed)

Word-style comment threads in a margin rail, aligned to the message they annotate, with collision pushdown and hover-linking.
